title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E555, §§35-43). Euler interpolates an odd curve y(x), with x = θω, through the nodes x = 0, ±nθ, ±(1−n)θ, ±(1+n)θ, ±(2−n)θ, … carrying the values 0, p, q, r, s, t, … . This node set is the union of the two shifted lattices Z+n and Z−n, plus 0. Corollary 1 of §36 gives

2nΔy/(n−ω) = Σ ±(value)/(k±n∓ω),

where Δ = B(n+ω, 1−n−ω)·B(n+ω, 1+n−ω)/B(n+ω, 1−2n).

This page.
(i) It finishes the list of four auxiliary sums from Euler's older work on partial-fraction expansions of cot and csc. The two families are
- 1/α − 1/(1−α) + 1/(1+α) − … = π cot απ;
- 1/α + 1/(1−α) − 1/(1+α) − 1/(2−α) + … = π/sin απ.
They are applied with α = n∓ω.
(ii) Example I (§40) takes values f, f, −f, −f, f, f, … . Regrouping the two rows of §36 by α = n−ω and α' = n+ω gives
2nΔy/(f(n−ω)) = π/sin(n−ω)π − π/sin(n+ω)π.
This simplifies to
2π cos nπ sin ωπ/(sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π) = 4π cos nπ sin ωπ/(cos 2ωπ − cos 2nπ).
(iii) Euler re-expresses Δ as an infinite product,
Δ = (1/(n+ω)) ∏_{k≥1} [k(k−2n)/((k−n)²−ω²)]·[k(k+2n)/((k+n)²−ω²)].
In modern terms this is
Δ = Γ(n+ω)Γ(1−n−ω)Γ(1+n−ω)Γ(1−n+ω)/(Γ(1+2n)Γ(1−2n)).
From the product he reads off where Δ has poles (ω = ±(i±n)) and where it vanishes (n = ±i/2).
(iv) Shifting ω by 1 gives Δ(ω+1) = −(1−n+ω)Δ/(n−ω). He also derives Δ(ω+2) = −(2−n+ω)Δ/(n−ω).
(v) §41-42: writing Δ = f(ω), the quantity f(ω)/(n−ω) is unchanged by ω → ω+i and by ω → −ω (more generally by ω → i−ω). In modern terms, Δ/(n−ω) = π²/(C sin(n+ω)π sin(n−ω)π) with C = 2nπ/sin 2nπ, which is 1-periodic and even. Euler has thus found the structure of the closed form that he proves as the Theorem of §44 on the following pages:
Δ = (n−ω)π sin nπ cos nπ/(n sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π).
Substituting it into (ii) gives y = f sin ωπ / sin nπ.
(vi) §43 links this to §25: put θ = π and f = sin nπ, so the nodes lie on the sine curve and the interpolant reproduces sin x. On the next page Euler stresses that this is not automatic, since infinitely many curves pass through the same points.

Purpose: to test whether his interpolation series on the double lattice Z±n reproduces trigonometric functions, and to obtain Beta-integral identities as a by-product.
errors: Euler says Δ is infinite whenever ω = ±(i±n) for any integer i. For i = 0 and ω = +n this is wrong: the factors k(k−2n) cancel and Δ(n) is finite (Γ(n+ω) has its pole only at ω = −n). This is a minor overstatement.

In the image as transcribed, III is given as = π/sin(n+ω)π and IV as = π/tang(n+ω)π. Mathematically III, whose signs simply alternate, should be π/tang(n+ω)π, and IV should be π/sin(n+ω)π. Either the print or the transcription has swapped them; the computation that follows correctly uses the csc-type sums (II and IV).

ideas.what: Partial-fraction (Mittag-Leffler type) expansions of π cot απ and π/sin απ, used with α = n±ω.
ideas.modern_name: partial-fraction expansions of cot and csc
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum I, ch. 10; earlier papers on series

ideas.what: Interpolation series on the node set {0} ∪ (Z+n) ∪ (Z−n), and the check that it reproduces sin πx for values sampled on the sine curve.
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange/cardinal-type interpolation on a union of two shifted lattices (second-order or periodic nonuniform sampling)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cardinal series: E.T. Whittaker 1915, Kotelnikov, Shannon. Two-coset (bunched) sampling: Kohlenberg 1953, Yen 1956
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula analytica I, 1783). Its presence in sampling-theory historiography is unsure.

ideas.what: Infinite-product expression for the ratio of Beta integrals Δ, equivalent to a product of four Gamma functions over Γ(1+2n)Γ(1−2n); its zeros and poles are read off from the product.
ideas.modern_name: Weierstrass product of 1/Γ together with the reflection formula
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Gamma products); Weierstrass for the canonical product
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on Beta/Gamma integrals and interpolation of products (e.g. E19, E321 and others)

ideas.what: Functional equations f(ω+1) = (n−1−ω)f(ω)/(n−ω) and f(−ω) = (n+ω)f(ω)/(n−ω). Together they mean Δ/(n−ω) is 1-periodic and even, which anticipates the closed form proved in §44.
ideas.modern_name: use of the recurrence and reflection of Γ to identify a periodic factor (a periodicity argument in the style of Liouville)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; such periodicity arguments are later standard (e.g. in proofs of Gamma identities)

missed.claim: Euler's interpolation on the nodes ±n, ±(1±n), ±(2±n), … is exactly interpolation on a union of two cosets of the integer lattice. It comes with an explicit closed-form kernel, sin ωπ/(sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π) times a periodic factor, and a proof that it reproduces sin πx. This anticipates the second-order (bunched / periodic nonuniform) sampling of Kohlenberg (1953) and Yen (1956). Standard histories of the sampling theorem (Butzer–Stens, Higgins) do not, to my knowledge, cite E555 for this. I am unsure.
missed.quote: Sint applicatae, quae abscissis nθ, (1−n)θ, (1+n)θ, (2−n)θ, (2+n)θ etc. respondent: p=f; q=f; r=−f; s=−f; t=+f
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It would push an early instance of two-coset interpolation, with an explicit kernel, back to Euler 1783 for historians of sampling theory and signal processing.

deep.surprise_reason: The algebra is correct and typical of Euler, and the Gamma/sine identities are classical. The modest interest is that the page amounts to explicit two-coset lattice interpolation reproducing sin, apparently not noticed in sampling-theory historiography. This is not a new theorem.
transcription_corrections: Left-hand side in §40: 'πΔy/(f(n−ω))' should read '2nΔy/(f(n−ω))', consistent with §36 and with the next page.
'ad II–IV' should probably read 'ad II et IV'; the two series reduce to formulas II and IV.
III and IV: the right-hand sides appear swapped. III (alternating) should equal π/tang.(n+ω)π, and IV should equal π/sin.(n+ω)π.

'cum autem ex superioribus sit Δ = 1/(π(n+ω))' is garbled. The sense is that, from the earlier products for Beta integrals, Δ can be written as the infinite product that follows; it does not equal 1/(π(n+ω)).

Product factors: they should be 1(1−2n)/((1−n)²−ω²) · 1(1+2n)/((1+n)²−ω²) · 2(2−2n)/((2−n)²−ω²) · 2(2+2n)/((2+n)²−ω²) · … . The transcription's '2(1+2n)' and '3(2+2n)' do not match the Gamma evaluation.
§41: 'si ω denotet numerum integrum' should read 'si i denotet numerum integrum'.
